title: SpaceX Hits 103 Falcon 9 Launches in 2026 with Another Starlink Mission
summary:
SpaceX continues its relentless pace of launches. Today, September 6, 2026, a Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 10:26 a.m. EDT, carrying 27 Starlink internet satellites into low Earth orbit. The launch occurred under clear blue skies—a rarity for the often foggy central coast.

About 8.5 minutes after liftoff, the rocket's first stage returned to Earth, landing on the drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You" in the Pacific Ocean. This was the 19th flight for this particular booster, designated B1088. That's impressive, but still short of the SpaceX record of 37 flights, set by B1067 on August 25.

The upper stage deployed the 27 satellites on schedule, about 62 minutes after launch. This mission was the 103rd Falcon 9 launch of 2026, with 80 of those dedicated to building out the Starlink megaconstellation. According to astronomer Jonathan McDowell, the network now consists of more than 11,000 active satellites, making it by far the largest satellite network ever assembled.

Starlink missions now fly exclusively from Vandenberg, as SpaceX has paused Florida launches until its Starship megarocket is operational. The company plans to use Starship to launch its next-generation Starlink V3 satellites, which are larger and more capable. Elon Musk has stated a goal of assembling a network of about 100,000 Starlink V3s in orbit.

This rapid cadence of launches is unprecedented in spaceflight history. Each Falcon 9 booster is reused multiple times, reducing costs and increasing launch frequency. As SpaceX continues to expand its satellite network, it raises questions about space debris and the impact on astronomy. But for now, the company shows no signs of slowing down.
why_it_matters: The internet and communications teenagers rely on are increasingly powered by thousands of satellites, but filling low Earth orbit this fast also means more space debris and brighter night skies — forcing this generation to decide how to balance connectivity, science, and safety in space.

background_read: SpaceX, the rocket company founded in 2002 by entrepreneur Elon Musk, has been trying to make rockets as reusable as airplanes — a complete break from half a century of spaceflight in which most boosters were thrown away after each flight.

Falcon 9 is the workhorse that made reuse routine: its first stage detaches, flips around, and lands itself on a robotic drone ship in the ocean or a landing pad on shore, and then flies again on later missions.

Vandenberg Space Force Base, located on California's often-foggy central coast, is a U.S. military spaceport whose location is well suited to the kind of polar orbits that the Starlink network uses for global coverage.
Starlink is SpaceX's own satellite-internet service; the network already serves remote homes, but astronomers complain that its bright moving trails can ruin long-exposure telescope images.

Jonathan McDowell, an astronomer who independently tracks what is in orbit and counts space debris, is often quoted about satellite growth, and his numbers have helped fuel debates about who should get a share of low Earth orbit.
SpaceX's next rocket, Starship, is much bigger than Falcon 9 and is expected to carry the heavier Starlink V3 satellites mentioned in the article.

perspectives.description: They benefit from cheaper launches, higher internet speeds in remote areas, and a business model built on reusing hardware. For them, rapid cadence is a success story: more launches mean more coverage and lower costs for customers.

They worry that thousands of bright satellites will streak through telescope images and hide faint stars, comets, and distant galaxies. Even with mitigations, the planned growth from 11,000 satellites to a possible 100,000 makes them anxious about the long-term future of ground-based astronomy.

They see an unprecedentedly crowded orbit with no globally agreed rules for who can launch how many satellites. The reuse revolution lowered costs so much that old assumptions about scarcity in orbit no longer apply, and regulators are struggling to catch up.

They are watching whether Starship and Starlink V3 actually deliver on their promises. If larger satellites include better deorbiting systems and darker surfaces, the next generation could build an even bigger network more responsibly — but only if the industry learns from the problems of the current one.
